children.text: kiṃ nu śayitā utasviduparataiva athavāntaḥkaraṇe'bhedaṃ prāptā āhosvid dravatāṃ yayau ityamunā saṃdehenānirvacanīyāvasthā ||
children.translated_text: One cannot describe what state she was in because of this doubt: “Is she perhaps asleep, or has she actually ceased to be, or has she attained non-difference within my heart, or has she melted away?”

children.text: madakalakalahaṃsacañcukoṭitroṭitakomalamṛṇālinīkisalayavatpariklāntair aṅgakaiḥ prābhātikanīlendīvaravanmukulitena locanayugalena vilayaṃ gacchantī nopalabdhetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: She was not perceived as she passed into dissolution, with limbs exhausted like tender lotus shoots snapped by the tips of the beaks of intoxicated, softly calling royal swans, and with her pair of eyes closed like a grove of blue lotuses at daybreak—this is the meaning.
For he too at that moment was nearly unconscious from bliss.
It explains, beginning with “gāḍha,” by what sequence she came to be in such a condition.

children.text: atinirbharāśleṣeṇāvāmanau vāmanau kṛtau yau kucau tatra prakarṣeṇodbhūtaḥ pulakodgamo yasyāḥ sā tathoktā ||
children.translated_text: She is so described because a pronounced eruption of horripilation appeared upon those two breasts that had been made small by an exceedingly tight embrace.

children.text: mā mā mānada mānakhaṇḍana mā atiśayena ||
children.translated_text: “No, no, O giver of honor, O breaker of pride, no—not so violently!”
In the expression “No, no, enough,” the half-spoken statement, lacking the verb “torments,” indicates agitation.
The repetition in “no, no,” and so forth is also beautiful.

children.text: atrāpi yadi kathyate tadā vadhū ruṣyati yadi maunāyate tadā gṛhaṃ naśyati ||
children.translated_text: Here too, if it is stated, the daughter-in-law becomes angry; if one remains silent, the household is ruined.

children.text: tathāpi karuṇabībhatsasmārakaṃ mṛteti padaṃ na mānayāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Even so, we do not accept the word mṛtā (“dead”), which evokes <s>karuṇa</s> (pathos) and <s>bībhatsa</s> (disgust).

children.text: tasmāt kiṃ mlānā śayitā nu kiṃ manasi me līnā vilīnā nu kim iti paṭhiṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore we shall read: “Has she perhaps lain down, faded? Has she merged into my mind? Or has she dissolved?”
“Where, with respect to one and the same object, there is doubt whose possible objects are multiple,
the perceiver’s uncertainty arising from similarity is called <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt).”
It explains what a newly married daughter-in-law does when amorous play begins for the first time.
